name: Lindrou
confidence_why: Martin's two-sentence SIL phonology sheet (data checked 1999, printed 2004; the same claim in Martin 1995) says stress generally falls on the first syllable, but Blust (2021), from his 1975 field notes, reports phonemic stress in disyllables with nine penultimate-versus-final minimal pairs (ális 'to caulk' / alís 'putty nut', láʔu 'leaf' / laʔúh 'two') and initial stress only in trisyllables, and his exemplified account outweighs an unexemplified summary.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records Lindrou as fixed initial (initial stress, from the SIL OPD sheet, Martin 1999: 'Stress genarally falls on the first syllable of multisyllable words'). The notebook's own transcriptions show final stress on a large share of disyllables (minék, madák, bohók, kusúk, lihík, balék, talóh, laʔúh, rinék) beside initial ones (bátuk, kápak, háhuw, ónoh), i.e. stress is not fixed initial in disyllables; trisyllables are mostly initial, which is the one part that agrees. This is the primary data behind Blust 2021 (index 1) and supports its 'phonemic stress' reading.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated anywhere in the packet; it is a wordlist with stress marked by acute accent. The marked data show that disyllables carry stress on either syllable (initial: bátuk 'head', kápak, háhuw 'four', ónoh 'six', rónoh 'ten'; final: minék 'hand', madák 'eye', bohók 'mouth', kusúk, talóh 'three', laʔúh 'two', rinék 'hundred'), so stress in disyllables is not predictable from position. Trisyllables are mostly initial (Kábesek, átabuk, mólosow, Kóloweh, bólobon) with exceptions (ndrohánoh '60'). Longer words carry an initial primary and a later secondary or the reverse (Kándrominèk, bólominèk, bóhokarèn). One explicit marginal note, '(Note stress)' beside ruwáni (item 678b, p.177), shows Blust flagging a non-initial trisyllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked in the notes with a grave on words of four or more syllables, e.g. Kándrominèk 'finger', bwísiminèk 'fingernail', bólominèk 'palm', bóhokarèn 'ridgepole' (p.170-171): initial primary, final secondary; no statement of a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions are stated; the data themselves show non-initial trisyllables (ndrohánoh '60', ndrohánek '600', ruwáni 'drop', badaʔán 'noon' p.175) beside initial ndróronoh '90'. The sentence sheets (pp. 179-181) carry almost no stress marks.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Blust items describe the Nyada-village variety of Lindrou (aka Nyindrou), speakers Bonin Boyap and Boluhe Soson, both 15, recorded 14-19 March 1975; the sheet header adds that the same language is spoken at Nihon, Kali, Lessau, Salien, Jowan, Korrojih and Bundrahi. The catalog's Martin/SIL source is labelled Sili-in, Manus Province. The Kaipuleohone record RB2-011 is a 29-language packet, not a Lindrou-only notebook: pp. 170-181 are Lindrou, p. 169 is the last Nauna sheet, p. 182 the first Pelipowai sheet (both downloaded only to confirm the boundary). The record lists no audio; the 'audio recordings' part of the citation is not on this handle.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog says fixed initial (Martin's OPD 1999 'generally first syllable, stem-initial after TAM prefixes'). Blust: stress is phonemic in disyllables (penult vs final minimal pairs), so 'fixed initial' fails for the disyllabic vocabulary; it agrees for trisyllables (initial by rule) and adds secondary-stress patterns and phrasal retraction. The 9/16 check row already recommends reclassification to 'contested / lexical in disyllables with initial default', keeping Martin as the dissenting source.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (contrastive) in disyllables, penult vs final, with nine minimal or near-minimal pairs (ális 'to caulk' vs alís 'putty nut', láʔu 'leaf' vs laʔúh 'two', lókkey 'jungle' vs loké 'up', etc.); trisyllables are nearly always initial (150+ items) and are left unmarked because statable by rule; words of four or more syllables carry a primary plus a secondary stress in recurrent 4/1 and 4/2 patterns. Historically Blust suggests final stress in disyllables arose by apocope of a penult-stressed trisyllable (Table 3.10, p. 231) but many forms resist that account.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.171: 'Words of more than three syllables, which are relatively uncommon, carry both a primary and a secondary stress.' Patterns: 4/1 (secondary on the 4th from the end, primary final: àli-kappá-, bòhokarén, kàdro-miné-), 4/2 (abùkuhássi, bàlakámus, màrigála), plus isolated 5/3, 5/2, 5/1, 4/3, 3/1; Blust cannot tell whether stress is phonemic in these words.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) A few trisyllables with penult or final stress: akoróh, badaʔán, ñabákow, ruáni, sakáro, tudrúdru (p.170). (b) Numerals 60-80 and 600-800 have penultimate stress on the base but 90/900 initial (drohánoh, drotónoh, drolúnoh vs dróronoh; p.170, p.173). (c) Final-stressed disyllabic stems shift to initial stress inside a phrase (baré-n 'its top' vs báre key 'top of a tree'; madá-n vs máda sur), with one counterexample bohó gwa (pp.170-171). (d) 17 disyllables from the sentence material have no recorded stress. (e) Geminates tend to follow stressed vowels but no causal link (p.171).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The works list has only one entry (index 0) and the compiler opened it, so there were no silent or not-opened works to spot-check. One small item the compiler index-0 summary understates: p.175 of the packet carries a second explicit stress annotation besides the '(Note stress)' at item 678 -- item 457 reads 'á:lis to caulk (cp alís 'putty nut')' with 'Note' underlined in the left margin, i.e. Blust flagged a penult-vs-final minimal pair in the field notes themselves (this is the ális/alís pair that heads Table 3.2 of Blust 2021). It strengthens, not changes, the lexical reading.

readall_conflicts: The catalog's fixed: initial syllable record rests on a two-sentence SIL Organised Phonology Data statement (Bill Martin, data checked 1999; same claim in Martin 1995 CAD): 'Stress genarally falls on the first syllable of multisyllable words. The main exception is in verbs with tense and aspectual prefixes.' Both Blust sources disagree for disyllables: the 1975 field sheets transcribe many disyllables with final stress (minék 'hand', madák 'eye', bohók 'mouth', talóh 'three', laʔúh 'two', rinék '100') beside initial ones (bátuk 'head', kápak, ónoh 'six'), and Blust 2021 states outright that Lindrou 'appears to have phonemic stress', backed by nine penult-vs-final minimal pairs, while agreeing that trisyllables are nearly always initial. The two Blust items do not conflict with each other (the sketch is the write-up of these sheets). Caveats on both sides: Blust's data are five days with two 15-year-old speakers from Nyada in 1975; Martin was a resident SIL fieldworker but gives no examples. Blust's phrasal retraction (final-stressed stems become initial inside a phrase, baré-n vs báre key) may partly explain why a fieldworker hearing connected speech would call the language 'generally initial'.

audit.recode_to: Drop 'fixed(-unreviewed) initial'. reclassify as contested/partly lexical: disyllables carry lexically contrastive stress (penult vs final, minimal pairs; Blust 2021 pp. 169-170), trisyllables regularly initial (150+ items), 4+-syllable words initial secondary with primary on the final or penult; final-stressed disyllabic stems retract to initial phrase-internally. Keep Martin OPD 1999 / CAD 1995 'generally initial, stem-initial after TAM prefixes' as the dissenting source in 'contra', with the fieldwork-depth caveat (Blust: 5 days, two teenage speakers, 1975; Martin: resident fieldworker, 2-sentence statement). If the catalog must keep a single class, 'lexical/unpredictable (disyllables) with initial default' is closer to the fuller source than 'fixed initial'.
